learn: The alphabet is all the letters we use to write. There are 26 letters. They go in order, from A to Z.
We can sing the letters to remember the order. A, B, C, D, E, F, G... Sing slowly and point to each letter as you sing it.
Every letter has a name. The first letter is A. The last letter is Z. M is in the middle.
check: How many letters are in the alphabet?
What is the first letter of the alphabet?
What is the last letter of the alphabet?
lessons.try: Sing the alphabet song and touch each letter on an alphabet chart as you sing.

learn: Each letter can be written two ways. The big one is called uppercase. The small one is called lowercase.
Uppercase B looks like this: B. Lowercase b looks like this: b. They have the same name and the same sound.
We use an uppercase letter at the start of a name, like Sam or Mia. Most other letters in words are lowercase.
check: What do we call a big letter?
What do we call a small letter?
Where do we use an uppercase letter?
At the start of a name
In the middle of every word
lessons.try: Find an uppercase and a lowercase letter in your name. Write them both.

learn: Letters are all around you. Look at signs, cereal boxes, books, and shirts. They all have letters.
A stop sign has the letters S, T, O, P. A box of milk has letters that spell milk.
Your name is made of letters too. The letters in your name are special to you. Learn to find them anywhere.
check: What letters are on a stop sign?
What is your name made of?
lessons.try: Go on a letter hunt in your room. How many letters from your name can you find?

learn: Letters have names, and they also make sounds. The letter m says /m/, like at the start of moon.
The letter s says /s/, like a snake: sssss. The letter t says /t/, like at the start of top.
When we know letter sounds, we can begin to read words. Sounds are the building blocks of reading.
check: Which letter sounds like a snake?
Why do we learn letter sounds?
lessons.try: Say the sound of m, s and t. Think of a word that starts with each one.

learn: Every word begins with a sound. Say dog slowly: d-o-g. The first sound is /d/.
Say fish slowly. The first sound is /f/. That sound goes with the letter f.
Good listeners stretch words out like a rubber band so they can hear each sound.
check: What is the first sound in dog?
What is the first sound in fish?
How can we hear each sound in a word?
Say it slowly, like stretching a rubber band
lessons.try: Say these words slowly and tell the first sound: ball, cat, pig.

learn: Some letters make sounds that are close. B says /b/ like ball. P says /p/ like pan.
Put your hand in front of your mouth. Say /p/. You feel a puff of air. Say /b/. Your throat buzzes a little.
D and T are close too. D says /d/ like dog. T says /t/ like ten. Listen closely to tell them apart.
check: Which sound makes a puff of air?
lessons.try: Say bat and pat. Which one starts with a puff of air?

learn: Five letters are special. They are called vowels: a, e, i, o, u.
Every word needs at least one vowel. The word cat has the vowel a. The word sun has the vowel u.
All the other letters are called consonants. B, c, d, f and g are consonants.
check: What do we call letters that are not vowels?
lessons.try: Clap once for each vowel as you say them: a, e, i, o, u.

learn: Short a says /a/ as in apple. Open your mouth wide and say /a/.
Short e says /e/ as in egg. Short i says /i/ as in itch, or in the middle of pig.
Listen for the vowel in the middle of small words. Cat has /a/. Pet has /e/. Sit has /i/.
check: What sound is in the middle of cat?
Short e says the sound in...
lessons.try: Say map, red and fin. Tell the vowel sound in each.

learn: Short o says /o/ as in octopus. Your mouth makes a round shape.
Short u says /u/ as in up and umbrella. It is a short, quick sound.
Hot has short o. Bug has short u. Now you know all five short vowels!
check: Short u says the sound in...
lessons.try: Say dog, mop, cup and bus. Sort them into short o words and short u words.

learn: Words rhyme when they end with the same sounds. Cat, hat and bat all rhyme. They end in -at.
Rhymes make songs and poems fun to say. "The cat sat on a mat" has lots of rhymes.
To check for a rhyme, say both words and listen to the end. Dog and log rhyme. Dog and cat do not.
check: Where do rhyming words sound the same?
lessons.try: Think of three words that rhyme with pig.

learn: You can make new rhymes by changing the first sound. Start with -ig. Add p for pig. Add w for wig. Add d for dig.
Rhymes can be silly words too. Jig, zig and fig all rhyme with big.
Poets choose rhymes to make their words sing. You can be a poet!
check: Change the p in pig to w. What word do you get?
Who uses rhymes to make words sing?
lessons.try: Make rhymes for -op: start with h, m and t.

learn: Words have parts called syllables. Each part is one beat, like a clap.
Dog has one clap. Ap-ple has two claps. But-ter-fly has three claps.
Put your hand under your chin. Your chin drops once for each syllable you say.
check: How many syllables are in dog?
How many syllables are in butterfly?
lessons.try: Clap the syllables in your name and in elephant.

learn: Reading means putting sounds together. This is called blending.
Look at m-a-p. Say /m/, /a/, /p/. Now say them faster and faster: map! You read a word.
Some readers move a finger under each letter as they say its sound, then slide the finger across to blend.
check: Putting sounds together to read a word
lessons.try: Blend these sounds: /s/ /u/ /n/. What word did you make?

learn: Many first words have three letters: a consonant, a vowel and a consonant. Teachers call them CVC words.
Cat, pen, dig, hop and bug are CVC words. Each has a short vowel in the middle.
When you see a CVC word, say each sound and blend. Soon you will read them fast.
check: What is in the middle of a CVC word?
Read h-o-p. What word is it?
lessons.try: Read these CVC words: pen, dig, hop.

learn: Change one sound and you make a new word. Cat becomes hat when you change /c/ to /h/.
Change the vowel and the word changes too. Hat becomes hit. Hit becomes hot.
Change the last sound. Hot becomes hop. Word ladders like this make you a strong reader.
check: Change the c in cat to h. What word do you get?
Change the a in hat to i. What word do you get?
Change the t in hot to p. What word do you get?
lessons.try: Start with pig. Change one sound at a time to make pin, then pan.

learn: Some words show up in books again and again. We call them sight words.
Good readers know sight words fast, just by looking. The, a, I, see, can, is and we are sight words.
When you know sight words, reading gets smoother and easier.
check: Words we know fast just by looking
Knowing sight words helps reading be...
lessons.try: Find the word the on a page of any book. How many times does it appear?

learn: Some sight words do not follow the usual sound rules. The word the is one. So are said and was.
We cannot always sound these words out, so we practise them until we just know them.
Look, say, spell and say again: s-a-i-d, said. That helps tricky words stick.
check: Which word is tricky to sound out?
How can we learn a tricky word?
Look, say, spell and say again
Is the word the a sight word?
lessons.try: Look at the word said. Say it, spell it aloud, then say it again.

learn: Sight words help us read whole sentences. "I can see a cat." Most of these words are sight words.
A sentence is a group of words that tells a whole idea. It starts with an uppercase letter and ends with a mark, like a period.
Point to each word as you read. Leave a little space between each word in your mind.
check: How many words are in "I can see a cat"?
lessons.try: Read this sentence and point to each word: We like to go.

learn: A book has a front cover, a back cover and pages. The cover protects the pages.
The title is the name of the book. It is on the front cover, usually in big letters.
The spine is the side that holds the pages together. On a bookshelf, you often see the spine.
lessons.try: Pick up a book. Point to the front cover, the back cover, the spine and the title.

learn: The author is the person who writes the words of a book.
The illustrator is the person who draws or paints the pictures.
Sometimes one person does both jobs. Beatrix Potter wrote and painted The Tale of Peter Rabbit.
check: Who wrote and painted The Tale of Peter Rabbit?
lessons.try: Look at a book cover. Find the names of the author and the illustrator.

learn: In English we read from left to right. We start at the top of the page and go down.
When we get to the end of a line, we sweep back to the left and start the next line.
We turn pages one at a time, from the front of the book to the back.
check: Which way do we read in English?
Where do we start on a page?
One at a time, front to back
lessons.try: Use your finger to show how your eyes move across a page.

learn: Characters are the people or animals in a story. In The Three Little Pigs, the pigs and the wolf are characters.
The main character is the one the story is mostly about.
Characters have feelings. They can be happy, scared, brave or silly. We learn about them from what they say and do.
check: The people or animals in a story
Who are the characters in The Three Little Pigs?
How do we learn about characters?
From what they say and do
lessons.try: Think of a story you love. Who is the main character?

learn: The setting is where and when a story happens.
A setting could be a farm, a city, a forest, a castle or under the sea. It could be at night or in winter.
Pictures often show the setting. Look at the trees, the houses and the sky.
check: Where and when the story happens
What often shows us the setting?
lessons.try: Draw the setting of your favourite story.

learn: A story has events. Events are the things that happen.
Something happens first, in the beginning. Then more happens in the middle. The story finishes at the end.
When we retell a story, we say the events in order: first, next, then, last.
check: The things that happen in a story
Which words help us retell in order?
lessons.try: Retell Goldilocks and the Three Bears using first, next, then and last.

learn: Some books tell made-up stories. We call them fiction. A talking bear is fiction.
Other books teach true facts. We call them nonfiction. A book about real bears and what they eat is nonfiction.
Nonfiction books often have real photos instead of drawings.
check: A book that teaches true facts
What do nonfiction books often have?
lessons.try: Find one fiction book and one nonfiction book. How can you tell?

learn: The topic is what the whole book is about. A book called Sharks has sharks as its topic.
Every page in a nonfiction book tells something about the topic.
Before reading, look at the cover and the pictures. Guess the topic.
check: What the whole book is about
What is the topic of a book called Sharks?
How can we guess the topic?
Look at the cover and the pictures
lessons.try: Look at a nonfiction book cover and say its topic.

learn: Good readers ask questions before, during and after they read.
Before: What do I think I will learn? During: What does this word mean? After: What was the most interesting fact?
Questions start with words like who, what, where, when, why and how.
check: When do good readers ask questions?
What was the most interesting fact?
lessons.try: Think of a question you would like a book about the moon to answer.

learn: Writers share their ideas with pictures and words.
First, think of your idea. Then draw it. Then add words that tell about your picture.
You can label your drawing. Write sun next to the sun and dog next to the dog.
check: What do writers use to share ideas?
Think of an idea and draw it
A word next to a picture that names it
lessons.try: Draw your favourite animal and label it.

learn: Say your sentence out loud first. Count the words on your fingers.
Write one word at a time. Leave a finger space between words.
A sentence starts with an uppercase letter and ends with a period, a question mark or an exclamation mark.
check: What do we leave between words?
With a period, question mark or exclamation mark
What should we do before writing a sentence?
lessons.try: Write the sentence: I like my cat.

learn: Writers share their work with others. They read it aloud, slowly and clearly.
Listeners can say one thing they liked and ask one question.
Writers can add more after sharing. Maybe add a word, a colour or one more sentence.
check: What can a writer do after sharing?
Add more to make it better
lessons.try: Read your writing to someone and ask them what they liked.
